campaign.title: The Lantern's Last Crew
campaign.hook: Your ship was somebody's before it was yours. Behind a panel, the crew finds a photo of its last crew, and on the underside of a bunk, a route scratched into the metal.

quay.name: Marrow Quay
quay.desc: A harbour moon of old stone docks and painted boats, where ships come to be mended and to rest.

mill.name: Coldwater Mill
mill.desc: A frosty little world with one village, one river and one enormous water mill that never stops turning.

orchard.name: Halloway
orchard.desc: A warm world of long gold grass and apple orchards that run all the way to the horizon.

episodes.title: Behind the panel
text: {Crew} is fixing a rattle behind a galley panel when something slides out and lands face down on the floor: a photograph, old and soft at the corners.

Five people squashed onto the steps of this very ship, laughing at something outside the frame. A tall woman in a captain's coat. A big bearded man holding a spanner like a bouquet. A cook with flour on her face. A thin, serious navigator. And a little girl on the cook's shoulders, missing two front teeth.
On the back, in pencil: "The Lantern's crew. Home is wherever we're all together."

episodes.title: The route
text: Once you know to look, there are traces of them everywhere. Initials carved inside a cupboard. A child's height marks on the doorframe of the smallest bunk, going up and up, year by year, with a name: Wren.

And on the underside of the top bunk, scratched into the metal with something sharp, a route: a line of dots joining five little drawings. A harbour. A mill. A tree with apples. A lighthouse. A heart.
Next to the harbour, in tiny letters: "Marrow Quay. Ask for Dory."

choice.prompt: Follow the scratched route, or put it back and leave their story alone?

options.label: Follow the route
options.reply: You trace the route onto paper and plot a course for Marrow Quay. {Crew} says it feels like being handed a letter that was always meant for you.

options.label: Leave it alone
options.reply: You put the photo back behind the panel. But that night {Crew} can't sleep, and in the morning the course is plotted anyway. Some letters want to be read.

episodes.title: Marrow Quay
text: {World} is all old stone docks and painted boats and the smell of tar and fried fish. Everybody here seems to know {ship} on sight. An old dockhand shades her eyes and says, "Well. She's back. Different crew, though."

Dory turns out to be the harbourmaster: tiny, ancient, and sharp as a hook. She looks at the photo for a long time. "Hesper Lane's crew," she says. "Best captain I ever moored. Your ship was theirs for thirty years. They brought her in here to be mended every spring."

episodes.title: Dory's stories
text: Dory tells you about them over a pot of black tea in the harbour office. Hesper, who could dock in a gale with one hand and a sandwich in the other. Bram the engineer, who sang to the engines. Juno the cook, who once fed the whole quay through a winter. Ottilie the navigator, who never got lost and never once smiled in a photograph.
"And Wren," Dory says. "Juno's girl. Born on that ship. Grew up on it. I never knew a child so in love with a place."
"Why did they give her up?" asks {Crew}. Dory looks into her tea. "Follow the route," she says. "It's not my story to tell."

episodes.title: The mill
text: The second drawing leads to {world}: a frosty village, a cold quick river, and a water mill so huge its wheel turns the whole village's life.

The miller is Bram. Older, his beard white now, but the same man from the photo, holding a spanner exactly the same way. When he sees {ship} land on the green outside his mill, he sits down very suddenly on a sack of flour.
"I hoped," he says. "Every spring I hoped. I put that route under the bunk myself. I always wondered who'd find it."

episodes.title: What Bram kept
text: Bram shows the crew around his mill as proudly as if he had built the river too. Then he takes them up to his attic, where there is one thing on a shelf: the old engine governor from {ship}, polished like silver.
"I swapped it out the year we left her," he says. "Kept it. Couldn't help it. Thirty years, I sang to that engine." He holds it out to {Crew}. "It should go home."

choice.prompt: Take the old engine part back to the ship, or tell Bram to keep it?

options.label: Take it home
options.reply: You fit it into {ship}'s engine before you leave. The engine starts with a sound it hasn't made in years: a low, contented hum, almost like someone singing.

options.label: Bram should keep it
options.reply: You fold Bram's hands back around it. "You kept her going thirty years," {Crew} says. "This is yours." Bram can't say anything for a while. He gives the crew a sack of his best flour instead.

episodes.title: Juno and Ottilie
text: Bram tells the rest, by his stove that night. Juno ran a bakery on the quay until she died, peacefully, ten years ago. Ottilie went home to her family's observatory and charts stars there still, and writes to him every winter.

"Hesper got old," he says. "Her hands shook. She couldn't fly any more, and she wouldn't let anybody else fly her ship while she was aboard. So we all stepped off, one by one, and left the Lantern for someone new. We hoped she'd find a good crew."
"And Wren?" asks {Crew}. Bram smiles. "Follow the route. The apples."

episodes.title: The heart on the map
text: Back aboard, the crew looks at the scratched route again. The harbour, the mill, the apples, the lighthouse, and at the very end, a heart. No name. No world.

text.text: In the engine room, the old governor Bram kept for thirty years hums along with the engine, steady and warm, as if the ship knows where it is going next.
In the galley there is a loaf of bread made from Bram's flour, and the whole ship smells of it, the way it must have smelled when Juno cooked here.

text: {Crew} touches the little heart with a fingertip. "I think it's not a place," {crew.they} {crew:says|say}. "I think it's a person."

episodes.title: Halloway
text: The apple tree on the route leads to {world}: long gold grass, warm wind, and orchards that roll all the way to the horizon, row after row, heavy with fruit.

At the edge of the biggest orchard is a farmhouse with a ship's bell hanging by the door. {Crew} recognises it at once: it is the bell from the photograph, the one Hesper is leaning against. It rings by itself in the wind, as if saying hello.

episodes.title: Wren
text: The woman who comes out of the farmhouse is about sixty, with apple leaves in her grey hair and two front teeth that are clearly not the originals. She looks at {ship}, and drops her basket, and walks very slowly across the grass with her hand over her mouth.
It is Wren. She puts her palm flat on the hull, the way you would on the cheek of somebody you had missed for a very long time. "Hello, old girl," she whispers. "Hello. You found a crew."

choice.prompt: Wren is standing by the hatch, not quite asking. Invite her aboard, or give her time?

options.label: Invite her aboard
options.reply: Wren walks through {ship} room by room, touching everything. She finds her height marks on the bunk door and laughs and cries at once. She sits on the little bunk for a long time.

options.label: Give her time
options.reply: You wait. Wren walks all the way around the ship twice, then sits in the grass beside it until the stars come out. Then she knocks on the hatch, very politely, like a guest.

episodes.title: Why they let her go
text: Over apple pie in the farmhouse kitchen, Wren tells the last of it. When Hesper couldn't fly any more, she wouldn't leave the Lantern either. She just sat on the bridge, day after day, holding the controls of a ship that never went anywhere.

"So I made her a deal," Wren says. "I'd stay with her here, on a world with apple trees, because she always wanted apple trees. And the Lantern would go to someone new. A ship that doesn't fly is a sad thing. I scratched the route so whoever got her would know she was loved."
"Is Hesper...?" begins {Crew}. Wren smiles and points out of the window, at the lighthouse on the hill.

episodes.title: The lighthouse on the hill
text: It is not really a lighthouse. It is a little stone tower Wren built on the hill above the orchard, with a lamp at the top that she lights every evening.
Hesper Lane is buried at its foot, under an apple tree. The stone says: "Captain. She brought everybody home."
"She asked me to keep a light on," Wren says, "in case the Lantern ever came back to see her." She looks at {ship} on the grass below. "And here you are."

episodes.title: What belongs to whom
text: Wren brings out a box from under her bed: the Lantern's first logbook, Hesper's captain's coat, and the brass nameplate that used to hang over the bridge door, polished every week for twenty years.
"These are the ship's," she says. "Not mine. Not any more. You're her crew now."

choice.prompt: Take the logbook, coat and nameplate back to the ship, or leave them with Wren?

options.label: Take them home
options.reply: The nameplate goes back over the bridge door, where its screw holes are still waiting. The coat hangs by the hatch. The logbook goes on the shelf above the captain's chair. The ship feels finished, somehow.

options.label: Leave them with Wren
options.reply: "They're yours too," {Crew} says. "You grew up in them." Wren holds the coat for a long time. Then she takes the nameplate off the box and hands it over anyway. "Just this," she says. "She should have her name."

episodes.title: One more trip
text: Wren hasn't been into space in forty years. On the last evening, {Crew} asks if she would like to go up, just once, just to orbit and back.

She sits in the navigator's chair, Ottilie's old chair, with her hands folded in her lap like a child on a birthday. When the ship lifts and the orchards fall away and the stars come out above {world}, she doesn't say anything at all. She just keeps looking.
When they land, she says, very quietly, "Thank you. I forgot how big it is. I forgot how small the farm is from up there. I like it both ways."

episodes.title: Home
text: Before {ship} leaves {world}, Wren scratches one more thing under the top bunk, beside the old route: a new line of dots, leading off the edge, to nowhere yet.
"That's yours," she says. "Your route. Make it a good one. And put a heart at the end of it, for whoever comes next."

text.text: As the ship lifts, the old engine governor hums its contented hum, and down on the hill the little tower's lamp comes on, and Wren rings the ship's bell, and rings it, and rings it.
As the ship lifts, down on the hill the little tower's lamp comes on, and Wren rings the ship's bell, and rings it, and rings it, until the sound is lost in the wind.

text: Somewhere in the galley, on the back of the old photograph, someone has added a line in fresh pencil, under the old one: "Still true."

lines.text: Wren keeps the lamp lit on the hill every evening. Some nights a ship flashes its lights back. It's usually {ship}.
Wren starts a small flying club in Halloway, for children, with an old one-seat shuttle and a lot of patience.
Bram builds a model of {ship} for his mill, with the old engine governor inside, and it hums when the river runs.
Bram listens for {ship} on the radio every spring, and sings to his mill wheel the rest of the year.

epilogue.name: Dory
lines: Dory finally retires from Marrow Quay at the age of a hundred and two, and hands the harbour keys to a girl who reminds her of Wren.

epilogue.name: Ottilie
lines: Ottilie writes to {ship} once, a single line, from her observatory: "I see you've been looking after her." She did not smile when she wrote it. Probably.

lines.text: The nameplate, the coat and the logbook stay aboard {ship}. The ship feels finished, and also just beginning.
The nameplate hangs over the bridge door. The coat and the logbook stay in Halloway, where somebody who grew up with them can hold them.
